entry.summary: ESTA under the Visa Waiver Program for tourism or business visits under 90 days. No paid or unpaid work, including volunteering, house-sitting or pet-sitting.
entry.max_stay: Under 90 days; the date on your I-94 record is the one that counts
entry.pre_arrival: Apply for ESTA. Be ready to answer questions about purpose, length, where you'll stay and your ties to Australia; officers may inspect devices and social media.
entry.other: A refused ESTA, a past refusal of entry or a stay over 90 days needs a visa interview at a US Embassy or Consulate in Australia. Some visa types require public social media settings. An onward ticket can't end in Canada, Mexico or the Caribbean unless you live there.

tourism.route: ESTA under the Visa Waiver Program

meetings.route: ESTA under the Visa Waiver Program
meetings.detail: Consulting with business associates is a permitted activity.
meetings.next: Be ready to explain the purpose at the border.

conference.route: ESTA under the Visa Waiver Program

unpaid-speaking.route: ESTA under the Visa Waiver Program
unpaid-speaking.detail: Speaking at a conference without payment is generally a business visit; officers decide at the border.
unpaid-speaking.next: Carry the invitation showing no payment beyond expenses.

paid-speaking.route: ESTA under the Visa Waiver Program (honorarium rules)
paid-speaking.detail: Speaking fees are allowed only from qualifying (mainly academic or nonprofit research) institutions, for no more than nine days at one institution and from no more than five institutions in six months; no salary from a US entity.
paid-speaking.next: Check the payer qualifies; otherwise a work visa is needed.

book-launch.route: ESTA under the Visa Waiver Program or a work visa
book-launch.detail: Promotion and readings may be business activity; paid appearances fall under the honorarium limits.
book-launch.next: Ask a US Embassy or an immigration lawyer.

ai-teaching.route: ESTA under the Visa Waiver Program (honorarium rules) or a work visa
ai-teaching.detail: Academic lectures can fit the honorarium rules; paid teaching for a company needs a work visa.

remote-work.detail: Not addressed on the pages read.

entrepreneur.route: ESTA under the Visa Waiver Program
entrepreneur.detail: Negotiating contracts and meeting partners fit; working in a US business needs a visa.

trade.route: ESTA under the Visa Waiver Program
trade.detail: Contract negotiation is a permitted activity.

artist.route: Performer visa (for example O or P)
artist.detail: Only amateurs taking part unpaid in musical or similar events fit the waiver.

mixed-mission.detail: The waiver covers business visits only; any work needs a visa.

filming.route: Media (I) visa for foreign media work
filming.detail: Representatives of foreign film or other information media are excluded from B-1 business visits.
filming.next: Ask a US Embassy which visa fits the filming you plan.

research.detail: Independent research may be a business visit; paid research at a US institution needs a visa.

volunteering.detail: Smartraveller notes that volunteering isn't allowed under the Visa Waiver Program.

laws.rule: Federal and state laws for drug-related offences vary, including laws related to the possession and recreational and/or medical use of marijuana (cannabis). Penalties for drug-related offences can be severe and often include minimum mandatory sentences. Some medications readily available in Australia are illegal or considered controlled substances in the US, even if prescribed by an Australian doctor. It's also illegal to possess any prescription medication without a prescription. See Health. US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) - Travelling with Medication
laws.heading: Drugs

laws.rule: The federal legal age for buying and drinking alcohol is 21 years old. State laws regarding the possession and consumption of alcohol can vary. Check the relevant state laws.
laws.heading: Alcohol

laws.rule: No federal law explicitly protects LGBTQIA+ people from discrimination, and not all state and local non-discrimination laws include protections based on sexual orientation or gender identity. Some states and localities have laws that may discriminate against or otherwise affect LGBTQIA+ travellers. Check relevant state and local laws. Although Australian passports comply with international standards for sex and gender, we can't guarantee that a passport showing 'X' in the sex field will be accepted for entry or transit by another country. Contact the nearest United States Embassy or Consulate before you travel for further information.
laws.heading: LGBTQIA+

laws.rule: Some US states have laws restricting access to abortion and other reproductive health care services. Research local laws and always consult your doctor before making any decisions about your medical care.
laws.heading: Abortion and reproductive health

laws.rule: Surrogacy laws can be complex. Get official legal advice from a US attorney before you agree to an arrangement.
laws.heading: International surrogacy

laws.rule: Some US states apply the death penalty for serious crimes. The death penalty can also apply to some serious federal offences, even if committed in states without capital punishment.

laws.rule: For specific information on bringing medication into in the United States, read the US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) - Travelling with Medication and US Food and Drug Administration (FDA).

laws.rule: While some US states will allow you to drive on your Australian driver's licence for a limited time, others require you to also have an International Driver's Permit (IDP). Some rental car companies also require you to have an IDP. You should get an IDP before you leave Australia. Digital driving licences are not yet widely accepted by rental car companies so travellers should carry a physical driving licence. money-and-cost.cash_card_notes: The local currency is the United States Dollar (USD). Declare all amounts over USD 10,000 (or its foreign equivalent) on arrival and departure. This covers all forms of currency, not only US dollars and not only cash. Failing to do so is a serious violation which can result in the seizure and forfeiture of your money. Criminal penalties can also apply. Banks and ATMs are widespread, and currency exchange services are available in most major cities and airports. Major credit cards are almost universally accepted.
